title: Lag synchronization field diary
content:
Purpose:
Quick exploratory notes to capture an odd p99/p999 pattern observed during multi-tenant bursts where requests appear temporally aligned (synchronized) and cause transient tail spikes beyond what simple queueing explains. Trying to capture experiment matrix, raw traces, and heuristics to reproduce.

High-level hypothesis:
- Some combination of arrival clustering + cache-thaw alignment is causing multiple in-flight requests to trigger worst-case kernel paths at the same time (KV cache misses + attention kernel fallback).
- Result: short-lived p99/p999 spikes (~50–300ms extra) that correlate with specific sequence-length distributions and cold-prefix patterns.

Experiment environment:
- Cluster: dev-gpu-pool-6 (A100x8 shards), runtime: canary-build-2025-09-10
- Model: gpt-small-open-quant (int8 dynamic), sequence lens: sampled from product traces (mean 128, tail to 1024)
- Clients: 200 parallel synthetic agents (poisson baseline) + 50 burst agents (synchronized wave), duration: 30m windows
- Metrics captured: per-request latency (end-to-end), server-entry timestamp, KV cache hit/miss, kernel path (fast/slow), GPU occupancy sample (10s), batch sizes

Run matrix (key variations):
1) Baseline poisson arrival (lambda tuned to target QPS=1200). cold-cache start. 30m.
2) Poisson + periodic micro-burst: every 60s a 200ms window where 120 agents send simultaneous requests.
3) Poisson + randomized start offsets for burst agents (uniform 0–20ms) to test alignment sensitivity.
4) As (2) but with KV prewarm (prefetch top prefixes) enabled.
5) As (2) but quantization fallback disabled (force slow kernel path on mismatch).
6) Fixed long prefixes (simulate long context continuation) vs short prompt-only requests.

Quick raw observations (notes-to-self):
- Run 1: baseline stable. p95 ~ 48ms, p99 ~ 83ms, p999 ~ 145ms. No obvious periodic spikes.
- Run 2: periodic spikes align with bursts. p99 jumps to 220–320ms for ~2–4 windows per 60s. Graph shows neat spikes (spike width ~ 150–400ms).
- Run 3: adding 0–20ms jitter reduced spike amplitude ~30% but did not eliminate tails. Suggests microsecond-level alignment matters but not the whole story.
- Run 4: KV prewarm drastically reduced amplitude (p99 ~100–120ms) but some spikes persist on long-seq requests — indicates two contributing factors (cache + kernel path).
- Run 5: forcing slow kernel path removed variance (everything high) — dives show that slow kernels dominate cost. But when both cache-miss and slow kernel coincide, worst-case multiplies.

Sampling of interesting spans (copied from logs):
- t=00:12:34.102 server-enter id=87321 latency=298ms kv_miss=true kernel=slow batch=64 seq_len=512
- t=00:12:34.103 server-enter id=87322 latency=305ms kv_miss=true kernel=fast batch=8 seq_len=32
- t=00:12:34.104 server-enter id=87323 latency=310ms kv_miss=true kernel=slow batch=128 seq_len=1024
Notes: three near-simultaneous requests, different batch sizes; suggests batching/coalescing decisions exacerbating overlap.

Telemetry correlation attempts:
- Correlate p99 spikes with: number of concurrent KV misses; fraction of slow kernels; CPU-side scheduling jitter; burst agent start timestamp alignment.
- Preliminary correlation: windows where >12 concurrent KV misses AND >40% slow kernel fraction => high probability of p99 spike. Thresholds need tuning.

Small micro-experiment (to test hypothesis about batching):
- Change batch-coalescing window from 5ms -> 1ms -> 10ms.
- 1ms: fewer large batches, reduced max latency but higher mean token-cost. p999 lowered by ~14% in bursts.
- 10ms: larger aggregations, GPU utilization improved but tails worse — more simultaneous slow kernel invocations.
- Tentative trade-off: narrow coalescing wins tails at expense of throughput/cost.

Quick sketches for charting (for later plotting):
- time-series: p50/p95/p99/p999 overlayed with concurrent_kv_misses and slow_kernel_fraction (dual axis)
- scatter: per-request latency vs batch_size color-coded by kv_miss
- CDFs: separate cache-hit vs cache-miss latency distributions during bursts

Immediate conclusions / actionable hypotheses:
1) Alignment of arrivals amplifies rare kernel paths; small jitter injection (1–5ms) helps but doesn't fully fix.
2) KV cache prewarm (prefix caching) reduces but some long-sequence or cold-prefix requests still trigger tails. Need adaptive prewarm policy based on arrival pattern.
3) Batch-coalescing window is a strong control knob — lower window reduces tails but raises cost. Propose an adaptive window: when burst detected drop to 1–2ms; otherwise allow larger window.
4) Build metric: "concurrent_kv_miss_count" and tie to autoscaling/fallback policies or temporary lane isolation.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Is the kernel path decision being made per-request or per-batch? (We suspect per-batch; need microtrace).
- How much of this is client-driven (simultaneous retries) vs server scheduling? Add synthetic run with randomized client retry backoffs.
- Try hybrid prewarm + on-demand micro-prefetch (first token only) to see quick win.
- Test on smaller model quant profiles to see if int8 fallbacks are more brittle to alignment.

Notes to self (ops):
- Create a short dashboard: p99 spikes annotated with concurrent_kv_miss_count and batch-coalescing-window value.
- Add a Linear ticket to prototype adaptive coalescing: RED-3502 (placeholder).

Rough todo (next 2 sprints):
- [ ] Add microtrace instrumentation for kernel-path-per-batch vs per-request (priority high).
- [ ] Implement simple jitter injection on ingress to test at scale (low-risk experiment).
- [ ] Prototype adaptive coalescing (1–5ms reduction during detected bursts).
- [ ] Run same experiment on dedicated pool (to ensure multi-tenant noise not main factor).

Unresolved items and wildcards:
- GPU memory pressure: saw slightly higher OOM logs during some windows — need to retest with memory profiling enabled. Could be unrelated but worth checking.
- Interaction with routing policy: if slow requests are routed to older-serving nodes, tails may be queueing there. Need to set routing to round-robin in test.

Freeform/brain dump (short):
- Maybe implement tiny randomized jitter per-connection seed at client-side on our SDK — can be an opt-in. Good trade for customers who care about tails.
- Consider "burst-detection" heuristic that flips coalescing and prewarm modes for 10–30s windows.
- If adaptive window reduces tails sufficiently, could backfill cost by raising base concurrency cap for those periods (still need econ analysis).

End notes:
- Keep this as a scratchpad; will convert to a short runbook if experiments converge.
- Share with Leo and Priya for sanity-check before broader rollout.
summary: Field diary capturing experiments around synchronized arrival-induced tail latency. Hypotheses: KV cache misses + synchronized batches + slow kernel path compound. Early mitigations: jitter, KV prewarm, adaptive coalescing windows. Next steps: microtrace kernel decision, prototype adaptive coalescing, test on dedicated pool.
